page: However, the consumption of ≥3 drinks has shown a biphasic effect on BP in which levels are decreased up to 12 hours after consumption and increased for 12 to 24 hours after consumption (systolic BP \[SBP\] increase, 3.7 mm Hg \[95% CI, 2.3–5.1\]).[37](#R37)A meta-analysis of 36 RCTs evaluating different levels of alcohol use in short- to medium-term crossover and parallel-group designs (2865 participants with and without hypertension) showed that consumption of <2 drinks/day compared with no alcohol use was not associated with a significant change in BP.[38](#R38) However, drinking ≥3 drinks/day resulted in significantly higher (increasing with higher alcohol consumption) SBP and diastolic BP (DBP) compared with no or less drinking. In participants who consumed ≥6 drinks/day and reduced their intake on average by ≈50%, strong reductions in SBP and DBP were observed (mean SBP and DBP differences, −5.5 mm Hg \[95% CI, −6.70 to −4.30\] and −3.97 mm Hg \[95% CI, −4.70 to −3.25\], respectively). These observational findings demonstrate the benefit of abstinence or a significant reduction in alcohol intake on increased BP.

page: The cohort studies and case-control studies (hereafter referred to as ‘conventional observational studies’) used in these meta-analyses are known to be subject to various types of bias when used to estimate causal relationships[11](/articles/s41467-024-47632-7#ref-CR11 "Hernan, M. A. & Robin, J. M. Causal Inference: What If. (CRC Press, 2023)."). First, neglecting to separate lifetime abstainers from former drinkers, some of whom may have quit due to developing preclinical symptoms (sometimes labeled ‘sick quitters’[12](/articles/s41467-024-47632-7#ref-CR12 "Marmot, M. Alcohol and coronary heart disease. Int. J. Epidemiol. 13, 160–167 (1984)."),[13](/articles/s41467-024-47632-7#ref-CR13 "Shaper, A. G., Wannamethee, G. & Walker, M. Alcohol and mortality in British men: explaining the U-shaped curve. Lancet 332, 1267–1273 (1988).")), and to account for drinkers who reduce their intake as a result of such symptoms may introduce reverse causation bias[13](/articles/s41467-024-47632-7#ref-CR13 "Shaper, A. G., Wannamethee, G. & Walker, M. Alcohol and mortality in British men: explaining the U-shaped curve. Lancet 332, 1267–1273 (1988)."). That is, the risk of IHD in, for example, individuals with low to moderate alcohol consumption may be lower when compared to IHD risk in sick quitters, not necessarily because intake at this level causes a reduction in risk but because sick quitters are at higher risk of IHD. Second, estimates can be biased because of measurement error in alcohol exposure resulting from inaccurate reporting, random fluctuation in consumption over time (random error), or intentional misreporting of consumption due, for example, to social desirability effects[14](/articles/s41467-024-47632-7#ref-CR14 "Davis, C. G., Thake, J. & Vilhena, N. Social desirability biases in self-reported alcohol consumption and harms. Addict. Behav. 35, 302–311 (2010).") (systematic error). Third, residual confounding may bias estimates if confounders of the alcohol-IHD relationship, such as diet or physical activity, have not been measured accurately (e.g., only via a self-report questionnaire) or accounted for. Fourth, because alcohol intake is a time-varying exposure, time-varying confounding affected by prior exposure must be accounted for[15](/articles/s41467-024-47632-7#ref-CR15 "Mansournia, M. A., Etminan, M., Danaei, G., Kaufman, J. S. & Collins, G. Handling time varying confounding in observational research. BMJ 359, j4587 (2017)."). To date, only one study that used a marginal structural model to appropriately adjust for time-varying confounding found no association between alcohol consumption and MI risk[16](/articles/s41467-024-47632-7#ref-CR16 "Ilomäki, J. et al. Relationship between alcohol consumption and myocardial infarction among ageing men using a marginal structural model. Eur. J. Public Health 22, 825–830 (2012)."). Lastly, if exposure to a risk factor, such as alcohol consumption, did not happen at random – even if all known confounders of the relationship between alcohol and IHD were perfectly measured and accounted for – the potential for unmeasured confounders persists and may bias estimates[11](/articles/s41467-024-47632-7#ref-CR11 "Hernan, M. A. & Robin, J. M. Causal Inference: What If. (CRC Press, 2023).").
quote: Second, estimates can be biased because of measurement error in alcohol exposure resulting from inaccurate reporting, random fluctuation in consumption over time (random error), or intentional misreporting of consumption due, for example, to social desirability effects[14] (systematic error).

page: It is well known that alcohol consumption increases the risk of morbidity and mortality due to many health conditions[1](/articles/s41467-024-47632-7#ref-CR1 "Bryazka, D. et al. Population-level risks of alcohol consumption by amount, geography, age, sex, and year: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2020. Lancet 400, 185–235 (2022)."),[2](/articles/s41467-024-47632-7#ref-CR2 "World Health Organization. Global Status Report on Alcohol and Health 2018. (World Health Organization, Geneva, Switzerland, 2019)."), with even low levels of consumption increasing the risk for some cancers[3](/articles/s41467-024-47632-7#ref-CR3 "Bagnardi, V. et al. Alcohol consumption and site-specific cancer risk: a comprehensive dose–response meta-analysis. Br. J. Cancer 112, 580–593 (2015)."),[4](/articles/s41467-024-47632-7#ref-CR4 "Wood, A. M. et al. Risk thresholds for alcohol consumption: combined analysis of individual-participant data for 599 912 current drinkers in 83 prospective studies. Lancet 391, 1513–1523 (2018)."). In contrast, a large body of research has suggested that low to moderate alcohol intake – compared to no consumption – is associated with a decreased risk of ischemic heart disease (IHD). This has led to substantial epidemiologic and public health interest in the alcohol-IHD relationship[5](/articles/s41467-024-47632-7#ref-CR5 "Goel, S., Sharma, A. & Garg, A. Effect of alcohol consumption on cardiovascular health. Curr. Cardiol. Rep. 20, 19 (2018)."), particularly given the high prevalence of alcohol consumption[6](/articles/s41467-024-47632-7#ref-CR6 "Manthey, J. et al. Global alcohol exposure between 1990 and 2017 and forecasts until 2030: a modelling study. Lancet 393, 2493–2502 (2019).") and the global burden of IHD[7](/articles/s41467-024-47632-7#ref-CR7 "Vos, T. et al. Global burden of 369 diseases and injuries in 204 countries and territories, 1990–2019: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2019. Lancet 396, 1204–1222 (2020).").
quote: It is well known that alcohol consumption increases the risk of morbidity and mortality due to many health conditions[1],[2], with even low levels of consumption increasing the risk for some cancers[3],[4].

page: A recent meta-analysis of the alcohol-IHD relationship using individual participant data from 83 observational studies[4](/articles/s41467-024-47632-7#ref-CR4 "Wood, A. M. et al. Risk thresholds for alcohol consumption: combined analysis of individual-participant data for 599 912 current drinkers in 83 prospective studies. Lancet 391, 1513–1523 (2018).") found, among current drinkers, that – relative to drinking less than 50 g/week – any consumption above this level was associated with a lower risk of myocardial infarction (MI) incidence and consumption between >50 and <100 g/week was associated with lower risk of MI mortality. When evaluating other subtypes of IHD excluding MI, the researchers found that consumption between >100 and <250 g/week was associated with a decreased risk of IHD incidence, whereas consumption greater than 350 g/week was associated with an increased risk of IHD mortality. Roerecke and Rehm further observed that low to moderate drinking was not associated with reduced IHD risk when accompanied by occasional HED[10](/articles/s41467-024-47632-7#ref-CR10 "Roerecke, M. & Rehm, J. Irregular heavy drinking occasions and risk of ischemic heart disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Am. J. Epidemiol. 171, 633–644 (2010).").
